analysis.one_liner: Requires trained, certified subprime mortgage lenders and bans forced arbitration in consumer contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required anyone providing subprime mortgage lending or brokerage services to pass a federal certification exam on subprime and predatory lending law, and allowed decertification of violators. It would have required lenders on high-cost mortgages to adopt a best-practices plan, resolve borrower complaints within 60 days without collecting on the loan during that window, and disclose every fee before closing, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for unfair or deceptive practices. It would also have made mandatory binding arbitration clauses in consumer contracts unenforceable, letting consumers go to court after a dispute arises, and funded $2 million a year in grants for community groups to educate borrowers about predatory lending.
analysis.who_benefits: Home buyers taking out subprime and high-cost mortgages, who were the primary targets of the abusive lending practices that fueled later foreclosures; consumers generally, who would regain access to courts instead of being forced into binding arbitration; and low-income neighborhoods, which would get funding for borrower education.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Subprime mortgage borrowers and consumers in arbitration-bound contracts

how_it_helps.text: Requires mortgage lenders and brokers serving subprime borrowers to pass a written certification exam covering federal lending law, subprime lending practices, and predatory lending practices, and lets HUD suspend or revoke certification from violators [S2] [S3].

Prohibits lenders from charging any fee on a high-cost mortgage that was not disclosed before the loan was signed, and requires plain-language disclosure of all charges and of the borrower's rescission rights at least 24 hours before closing [S2] [S3].

Requires lenders on high-cost mortgages to make a good-faith effort to resolve consumer complaints within 60 days, during which they may not collect on the loan or enforce it against the borrower's property [S3].
Makes unfair or deceptive acts in subprime lending unlawful, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for a first violation and $20,000 per day for repeat violations [S2] [S3].

Declares unenforceable any pre-written clause in a consumer contract requiring binding arbitration, restoring consumers' ability to take disputes to court (agreements made voluntarily after a dispute arises remain allowed) [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $2 million per year in grants to nonprofit community development corporations to educate borrowers and community groups about illegal and inappropriate predatory lending practices [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers, who would bear the cost of certification exams, employee training plans, complaint resolution, stricter fee disclosure, and per-day civil penalties; arbitration providers, whose mandatory pre-dispute clauses in consumer contracts would become unenforceable; and taxpayers, who would fund the small grant and training appropriations. Some of the lenders' compliance costs could be passed to subprime borrowers through higher loan prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subprime lenders, brokers, and arbitration providers

drawbacks.text: Certification and training requirements add compliance costs that subprime lenders could pass on to the very borrowers the bill aims to protect, and some lenders might stop serving riskier borrowers rather than bear them [S3].

The arbitration ban applies to all consumer contracts, not just mortgages, which is far broader than the bill's title suggests and would eliminate a dispute channel many businesses consider faster and cheaper than litigation [S2] [S3].

The bill leans heavily on HUD to define 'predatory lending' and set certification standards within six months, leaving the actual protective force dependent on how a future administration wrote those rules [S3].
The education grants are small — $2 million per year — relative to the scale of the lending markets involved [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subprime borrowers and consumers, the protections were substantial: trained loan officers, no surprise fees, a complaint window before collection, per-day penalties, and court access instead of forced arbitration. The honest costs are that certification and complaint-handling requirements raise lenders' expenses, some of which would flow into loan prices, and the arbitration ban's reach beyond mortgages was broad enough to draw legitimate business objection. On balance the bill was designed to shift risk from borrowers to lenders, and the modest grant funding limited its cost to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2005 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephanie Tubbs Jones of Ohio introduced the Predatory Mortgage Lending Practices Reduction Act on April 28, 2005, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S3] [S5].
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors, 30 Democrats and 1 Independent, but no recorded Republican support [S4].
The action history shows no activity after the referral: the committee never reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber [S5].
The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without ever leaving committee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers are better off because the bill died: they avoided federal certification exams, mandatory best-practices plans, 60-day complaint-resolution freezes on collection, strict fee disclosure, and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day. Arbitration providers likewise kept pre-dispute mandatory arbitration clauses enforceable in consumer contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subprime lenders, brokers, and arbitration providers

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Tubbs Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 28, 2005, to require certification of subprime mortgage lenders, restrict unfair fees, and ban mandatory arbitration in consumer contracts.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors (30 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. DeLauro, Cummings, Millender-McDonald, Grijalva, Owens, Kilpatrick, Jefferson, and Jackson as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after receiving the bill: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and never reported it to the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 109th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every recorded supporter was a Democrat or Independent — the sponsor and 31 cosponsors (30 D, 1 I) — with no Republican cosponsors, and the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican during that Congress.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to pass a federal certification exam, maintain best-practices plans, disclose every fee before closing, freeze collection during 60-day complaint windows, and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per day — costs borne by an industry whose profits often came from exactly the fees and practices the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and consumer-credit industries relying on mandatory arbitration
industries.note: The Consumer Fairness Act title would have made pre-dispute binding arbitration clauses unenforceable in all consumer contracts, ending a system in which consumers sign away their day in court as a condition of getting credit.
The bill authorized $2 million per year in grants to fund borrower and community education about predatory lending practices.
